writing.prompt: Directions: Suppose the university newspaper is inviting submissions from the students for its coming edition on what in their university impresses them most.You are now to write an essay for submission. You will have 30 minutes to write the essay. You should write at least 120 words but no more than 180 words.
writing.sample: Among the many things on campus, it is the university library that has impressed me most. While my college offers modern labs and lively clubs, none of them stays in my heart as deeply as that quiet building.Quiet and well-lit, the library offers a space where I can truly focus and lose myself in books. Surrounded by towering shelves, I felt the joy of learning for the very first time. What touched me even more was a small experience. I still remember the day when I was searching desperately for an out-of-print book. It was a gentle old librarian who spent half an hour helping me track it down, which made me realize that this place is warmed not only by knowledge but also by kindness.Looking back, the library is more than a study room; it has taught me to seek knowledge actively rather than passively. That is why this quiet corner will always be the most unforgettable part of my university life.

transcript.en: Have you noticed how similar you are to your friends? It may be because your brains operate in harmony with each other. We know that friends are more likely to be the same age, gender and ethnic background as each other. Now it seems their brains are alike, too.
transcript.zh: 你有没有注意到你和朋友有多相似?这可能是因为你们的大脑彼此协调运作。我们知道朋友之间更有可能拥有相同的年龄、性别和种族背景。现在看来他们的大脑也很相似。

transcript.en: Researchers at the University of California scanned the brains of 42 classmates while they watched videos intended to provoke varying responses. Some people might find a romantic scene touching, for instance, while others would feel it was embarrassing. The activity of friends' brains was more similar than that of people who didn't know each other, particularly in regions involved in attention, emotion and language. This similarity was strong enough that it could be used to predict whether two people were already friends or not. The relationship probably goes two ways. We are drawn to people who think like us; we then influence their thoughts over time, which may push their brain activity into more closely resembling our own.
transcript.zh: 加利福尼亚大学的研究人员扫描了42名同学的大脑,同时让他们观看旨在引发不同反应的视频。例如,有些人可能会觉得浪漫场景令人感动,而另一些人则会觉得尴尬。朋友大脑的活动比不认识的人更相似,特别是在涉及注意力、情绪和语言的区域。这种相似性强到足以用来预测两个人是否已经是朋友。这种关系可能是双向的。我们会被那些思维方式与我们相似的人所吸引;随着时间的推移,我们会影响他们的想法,这可能会促使他们的大脑活动更接近我们自己的。

transcript.en: Two men who have been best friends for 60 years have just realized they are actually brothers. It's reported that Alan Robinson and Walter MacDonald met in the 6th grade at a school in Hawaii. They have been best friends ever since. Alan was given away for adoption soon after he was born, and Walter never knew his father. So recently, they made separate attempts on DNA matching websites to discover more about their ancestry. Walter was astonished to find that he matched with website user Robi 737. He knew immediately that this was his best friend Alan, whose friends call him Robi and flew 737 airplanes when he was a pilot. The pair were born to the same mother 15 months apart.
transcript.zh: 两名保持了60年最佳友谊的男子刚刚意识到他们实际上是兄弟。据报道，Alan Robinson和Walter MacDonald在夏威夷的一所学校读六年级时相识。从那时起他们就一直是最好的朋友。Alan出生后不久就被送去领养，而Walter从未见过自己的父亲。因此最近，他们分别在DNA匹配网站上尝试了解更多关于自己祖先的信息。Walter惊讶地发现他与网站用户Robi 737匹配。他立即知道这就是他最好的朋友Alan，Alan的朋友们都叫他Robi，而且他当飞行员时驾驶737飞机。这对朋友出生于同一位母亲，相隔15个月。

transcript.en: A man passing by decided to video their good deed and put it on the internet. It was unclear where the rest of the group was from, but they were most likely traveling together. One local woman commented on being embarrassed that tourists were cleaning up their beach. Another mentioned that it was actually the natives who brought food and drinks then left trash all along the island.
transcript.zh: 一名路过的男子决定录下他们的善举并放到网上。目前还不清楚这个团队其余成员来自哪里,但他们很可能是一起旅行的。一位当地女性评论说,游客在清理他们的海滩让她感到尴尬。另一个人提到,实际上是本地人带来食物和饮料,然后把垃圾留在整个岛上。

transcript.en: W: Hello Benjamin, Dan and I will be going for a run along the canal Saturday morning. Would you like to join us?
transcript.zh: W: 你好 Benjamin,我和 Dan 周六早上要沿着运河跑步。你想一起来吗?

transcript.en: M: I'd love to, but I hurt my ankle last weekend playing football with work colleagues.
transcript.zh: M: 我很想去,但我上周末和同事踢足球时伤了脚踝。

transcript.en: W: Oh dear, is it serious?
transcript.zh: W: 哎呀,严重吗?

transcript.en: M: No, not at all. I landed badly during a fall and twisted it a little, but it's no big deal. It's just a little swollen and I should be fine for next Saturday if you still want to go for a jog then.
transcript.zh: M: 不,一点也不严重。我摔倒的时候落地不太好,扭了一下,但不是什么大事。只是有点肿,下周六应该就没事了,如果你那时候还想去慢跑的话。

transcript.en: W: I won't be here next Saturday. I'm going to the zoo.
transcript.zh: W: 我下周六不在这儿。我要去动物园。

transcript.en: M: The zoo?
transcript.zh: M: 动物园?

transcript.en: W: Yeah. My little nephew turns six, and he loves the zoo, so the whole family is going.
transcript.zh: W: 对。我小侄子要过六岁生日了,他很喜欢动物园,所以全家人都要去。

transcript.en: M: Oh, okay then. I haven't been to a zoo since I was a kid.
transcript.zh: M: 哦,好吧。我从小时候起就没去过动物园了。

transcript.en: W: They are nowhere near as popular as they used to be when we were children. I personally feel sorry for the poor animals stuck in cages, but there's no denying they are fun and educational for children.
transcript.zh: W: 动物园远不像我们小时候那么受欢迎了。我个人觉得那些被关在笼子里的可怜动物很可怜,但不可否认的是,它们对孩子们来说既有趣又有教育意义。

transcript.en: M: Do you know if Dan will be around next Saturday?
transcript.zh: M: 你知道 Dan 下周六有空吗?

transcript.en: W: Yeah, I think he will. Just send him a text message. He's always keen on physical activities.
transcript.zh: W: 嗯,我觉得他应该有空。给他发个短信吧。他总是很热衷于体育活动。

transcript.en: M: That's true. Dan is extremely fit and healthy. He goes to the gym most days, plus tennis two or three times a week.
transcript.zh: M: 没错。Dan 身体特别好。他几乎每天都去健身房,再加上每周打两三次网球。

transcript.en: W: So, what have you been doing to stay busy while you've had that swollen ankle?
transcript.zh: W: 那么,你脚踝肿的这段时间都在忙些什么呢?

transcript.en: M: I've been catching up on some reading. I was given three books over Christmas, and I'm only now getting around to reading them.
transcript.zh: M: 我一直在补看一些书。圣诞节的时候收到了三本书,现在才开始读。

transcript.en: W: Our guest on today's Book Talk is John Black, the author of the new bestseller, Retire Early.

transcript.en: M: Thanks for having me on the show, Lisa.
transcript.zh: M: 谢谢邀请我来节目，Lisa。

transcript.en: W: John, your book is getting a lot of attention, partly because you write that most people can retire by 40. Is that realistic?
transcript.zh: W: John，你的书正受到很多关注，部分原因是你在书中写到大多数人可以在 40 岁退休。这现实吗？

transcript.en: M: Definitely. When researching this book, I interviewed hundreds of people who retired by 40.
transcript.zh: M: 绝对现实。在研究这本书时，我采访了数百位在 40 岁前退休的人。

transcript.en: W: Okay, but how much money does a person need to retire? I've read articles recommending one million dollars as a good figure for retirement.
transcript.zh: W: 好吧，但是一个人需要多少钱才能退休？我读过一些文章推荐一百万美元作为退休的合适数字。

transcript.en: M: While most financial planners do give numbers, I don't think that's useful, as people are living in different areas with different costs of living, and have different needs and wants, which is why I suggest that people aim for financial independence.
transcript.zh: M: 虽然大多数理财规划师确实会给出具体数字，但我认为那没什么用，因为人们生活在不同地区，生活成本不同，需求和期望也不同，所以我建议人们以财务独立为目标。

transcript.en: W: What do you mean by financial independence?
transcript.zh: W: 你说的财务独立是什么意思？

transcript.en: M: Having investment income that's greater than monthly expenses.
transcript.zh: M: 就是投资收入大于月度开销。

transcript.en: W: That sounds risky to me. What if an accident happens or you get ill and need medical treatment? Shouldn't people have extra cash for emergencies?
transcript.zh: W: 这在我看来有点冒险。如果发生意外或者生病需要医疗怎么办？人们不应该留些额外现金以备不时之需吗？

transcript.en: M: Too many people spend their lives working on jobs they hate because they're afraid, so I counsel people to take risks. Retirement doesn't have to be permanent, and if people need to, they can go back to work.
transcript.zh: M: 太多人因为恐惧而一辈子做着自己讨厌的工作，所以我建议人们去冒险。退休不一定是永久的，如果需要，人们可以重返工作。

transcript.en: W: But it's not always easy to get back into the workforce after an extended absence.
transcript.zh: W: 但是长时间离开职场后再回去并不总是那么容易。

transcript.en: M: True, but if you keep current with your skills, you will be attracted to employers.
transcript.zh: M: 确实，但如果你保持技能更新，你会对雇主有吸引力的。

transcript.en: W: Maybe, but how can anyone save enough to retire by 40 when most people can't retire at 60?
transcript.zh: W: 也许吧，但大多数人 60 岁都退不了休，怎么可能有人能存够钱在 40 岁退休呢？

transcript.en: M: Simple, by cutting housing, food, and transport expenses, and investing half your monthly income.
transcript.zh: M: 很简单，削减住房、食物和交通开支，然后把月收入的一半用于投资。

transcript.en: W: That sounds impossible.

transcript.en: M: I admit it's difficult, but it has worked for thousands.
transcript.zh: M: 我承认很难，但对成千上万的人确实有效。

transcript.en: New research from America studies the role that the presence of individuals from different social or racial groups has in influencing consumers' food choices. This research found college students were more likely to choose healthy food in the presence of an observer of a different race, as opposed to an observer from their own race. The same was true when they were with someone from a different university, compared to someone from their own. Researchers say this was because participants anticipated more negative judgment from an outsider group. In contrast, they felt less judged by members of their own group.
transcript.zh: 来自美国的新研究探讨了来自不同社会或种族群体的个体的存在对消费者食物选择的影响作用。该研究发现,与同种族观察者在场相比,大学生在不同种族观察者在场时更有可能选择健康食品。当他们与来自不同大学的人在一起时,情况也是如此,而不是与来自自己大学的人在一起时。研究人员表示,这是因为参与者预期会受到外部群体更多的负面评判。相比之下,他们感到受到自己群体成员的评判较少。

transcript.en: In one experiment, participants were offered the choice between candy and fruit as a snack. When in the presence of an unknown student from their own university, only 12 percent of students selected the healthier option. However, this number was 31 percent when in the presence of an unknown student from another university. Other experiments showed similar results based on racial group.
transcript.zh: 在一项实验中,参与者可以选择糖果或水果作为零食。当与一名来自自己大学的陌生学生在场时,只有12%的学生选择了更健康的选项。然而,当与一名来自另一所大学的陌生学生在场时,这一数字为31%。其他基于种族群体的实验显示了类似的结果。

transcript.en: What's the reason for this pattern? The study found that people feel judged to a larger extent by members of other groups. Because of this, they strategically use healthy food choices to make a positive impression. There have been many attempts to help consumers make healthier choices, but consumers often struggle to maintain a healthy diet. This research finds that one way to promote a healthy diet could be to advertise the social benefits of healthy choices.
transcript.zh: 这种模式的原因是什么?该研究发现,人们感到在更大程度上受到其他群体成员的评判。因此,他们策略性地使用健康食品选择来留下积极印象。已经有许多尝试帮助消费者做出更健康的选择,但消费者往往难以保持健康饮食。该研究发现,促进健康饮食的一种方法可能是宣传健康选择的社会益处。

transcript.en: For college students under pressure, a dog may be the best stress fighter around, according to the finding of a recent study. "It's a really powerful finding," said Patricia Pendry, who led the study. "Universities are doing a lot of great work trying to help students succeed academically, especially those who may be at risk due to a history of mental health issues or academic and learning issues. This study shows that traditional stress management approaches aren't as effective for this population compared with programs that focus on providing opportunities to interact with therapy dogs."
transcript.zh: 根据最近一项研究的发现，对于压力之下的大学生来说，狗可能是最好的压力克星。领导这项研究的Patricia Pendry说："这是一个非常有力的发现。大学正在做大量出色的工作来帮助学生在学业上取得成功，尤其是那些可能因心理健康问题史或学业和学习问题而处于风险中的学生。这项研究表明，传统的压力管理方法对这一群体的效果不如那些专注于提供与治疗犬互动机会的项目。"

transcript.en: The researchers measured executive functioning in the students involved in the study. Executive function is a term for the skills one needs to plan, organize, motivate, concentrate and memorize. These are skills students need to succeed in college. The researchers found that students who were most at risk had the most improvements in executive functioning after interacting with therapy dogs. These results remained when researchers followed up six weeks later.
transcript.zh: 研究人员测量了参与研究的学生的执行功能。执行功能是指一个人计划、组织、激励、集中注意力和记忆所需的技能。这些是学生在大学取得成功所需要的技能。研究人员发现,风险最高的学生在与治疗犬互动后,执行功能改善最大。当研究人员在六周后进行随访时,这些结果仍然保持。

transcript.en: Many universities provide academic stress management programs and workshops. These are traditionally very similar to college classes. They often talk about ways to get more sleep, set goals, or manage stress or anxiety. Pendry acknowledges that these are really important topics and these workshops help typical students succeed. But they're less helpful for struggling students. Pendry believes those students may experience the programs as another lecture and feel even more stressed.
transcript.zh: 许多大学提供学业压力管理项目和研讨会。这些传统上与大学课程非常相似。它们通常讨论如何获得更多睡眠、设定目标或管理压力或焦虑的方法。Pendry承认这些是非常重要的话题,这些研讨会帮助典型学生取得成功。但它们对挣扎中的学生帮助较小。Pendry认为,那些学生可能会将这些项目体验为又一次讲座,并感到更加紧张。

transcript.en: Taking risks in business does not mean going into business blindly and then expecting great results. On the contrary, taking risks in entrepreneurship involves careful planning and hard work. Nobody can really be sure if risks will be met with success, no matter how calculated they may be. But this should not stop you from taking risks, as risks are necessary if you want your business to succeed.
transcript.zh: 在商业中冒险并不意味着盲目创业然后期待巨大的成果。相反,创业中的冒险涉及周密的计划和艰苦的工作。无论风险计算得多么仔细,没有人能真正确定风险是否会获得成功。但这不应该阻止你冒险,因为如果你想让企业成功,冒险是必要的。

transcript.en: Some risks may not work out, but an optimistic risk-taker will always look at failure as an opportunity to learn. The willingness to experiment with new ideas is key to business growth. As the old saying goes, "Nothing ventured, nothing gained." Failure will teach you how to think and plan strategically. But just remember that not all risks are good ones, and when you fail, learn from it and move forward.
transcript.zh: 有些风险可能不会成功,但乐观的冒险者总是将失败视为学习的机会。愿意尝试新想法是企业成长的关键。正如老话所说,"不入虎穴,焉得虎子。"失败会教你如何进行战略思考和规划。但要记住,并非所有风险都是好的,当你失败时,要从中吸取教训并继续前进。

transcript.en: Since most people tend to avoid risk, businesses that are brave enough to take risks already have a competitive advantage. They are the ones setting the standard with new ideas, fresh offers and bold inventions. Risk-takers are best at adapting in difficult times. Simply put, when most individuals stay away from risk, it means less competition for risk-takers. We don't know if you'll achieve what these risk-takers have achieved. But for as long as you want to stay safe, and for as long as you are content with where your business is right now, you will never find out.
transcript.zh: 由于大多数人倾向于规避风险,那些勇于冒险的企业已经拥有了竞争优势。他们用新想法、新颖的产品和大胆的发明树立标准。冒险者最善于在困难时期适应。简单地说,当大多数人远离风险时,这意味着冒险者面临的竞争更少。我们不知道你是否能取得这些冒险者所取得的成就。但只要你想保持安全,只要你满足于企业目前的状况,你就永远不会知道答案。

passage.t: When people set out to improve their health, they usually take a familiar path: starting a healthy diet, getting better sleep, and doing regular exercise. Each of these behaviors is important, of course, but they all
on physical health—and a growing body of research suggests that social health is just as, if not more, important to
well-being. One recent study published in the journal PLOS ONE, for example, found that the strength of a person's social circle was a better
of self-reported stress, happiness and well-being levels than fitness tracker data on physical activity, heart rate and sleep. That finding suggests that the "
self" represented by endless amounts of health data doesn't tell the whole
. There's also a qualified self, which is who I am, what are my activities, my social network, and all of these aspects are not
in any of these measurements. This idea is supported by plenty of
research. Studies have shown that social support—whether it comes from friends, family members or a spouse—is

associated with better mental and physical health. A rich social life, these studies suggest, can lower stress levels, improve mood, encourage positive health behaviors and discourage damaging ones, boost heart health and improve illness
rates. Social isolation, meanwhile, is linked to higher rates of physical diseases and mental health conditions. It's a significant problem,
since loneliness is emerging as a widespread public health problem in many countries.

paragraphs.t: As a parent of two boys at primary school, I worry about the issues associated with teenagers and social media. Newspapers are constantly filled with frightening accounts of drug addiction and aggressive behaviour supposedly caused by violent video games. But even when these accounts touch on real concerns, they do not really reflect the great mass of everyday teenage social behaviour: the online chat, the texting, the surfing, and the emergence of a new teenage sphere that is conducted digitally.

New technologies always provoke generational panic, which usually has more to do with adult fears than with the lives of teenagers. In the 1930s, parents worried that radio was gaining "an irresistible hold of their children". In the 80s, the great danger was the Sony Walkman(随身听). When you look at today's digital activity, the facts are much more positive than you might expect.

Indeed, social scientists who study young people have found that their digital use can be inventive and even beneficial. This is true not just in terms of their social lives, but their education too. So if you use a ton of social media, do you become unable, or unwilling, to engage in face-to-face contact? The evidence suggests not. Research by Amanda Lenhart of the Pew Research Centre, a US think tank, found that the most passionate texters are also the kids most likely to spend time with friends in person. One form of socialising doesn't replace the other. It expands it.

"Kids still spend time face to face," Lenhart says. Indeed, as they get older and are given more freedom, they often ease up on social networking. Early on, the web is their "third space", but by the late teens, it's replaced in reaction to greater independence. They have to be on Facebook, to know what's going on among friends and family, but they are ambivalent(有矛盾心理的) about it, says Rebecca Eynon, a research fellow at the Oxford Internet Institute, who has interviewed about 200 British teenagers over three years. As they gain experience with living online, they begin to adjust their behaviour, struggling with new communication skills, as they do in the real world.

Parents are wrong to worry that kids don't care about privacy. In fact, they spend hours changing Facebook settings or using quick-delete sharing tools, such as Snapchat, to minimise their traces. Or they post a photograph on Instagram, have a pleasant conversation with friends and then delete it so that no traces remain.

This is not to say that kids always use good judgment. Like everyone else, they make mistakes—sometimes serious ones. But working out how to behave online is a new social skill. While there's plenty of drama and messiness online, it is not, for most teens, a cycle of non-stop abuse: a Pew study found only 15% of teens said someone had bullied them online in the last 12 months.

But surely all this short-form writing is affecting literacy? Certainly, teachers worry. They say that kids use overly casual language and text-speak in writing, and don't have as much patience for long reading and complex arguments. Yet studies of first-year college papers suggest these anxieties may be partly based on misguided nostalgia(怀旧). When Stanford University scholar Andrea Lunsford gathered data on the rates of errors in "freshman composition" papers going back to 1917, she found that they were virtually identical to today.

But even as error rates stayed stable, student essays have blossomed in size and complexity. They are now six times longer and, unlike older "what I did this summer" essays, they offer arguments supported by evidence. Why? Computers have vastly increased the ability of students to gather information, sample different points of view and write more fluidly.

When linguist Naomi Baron studied students, instant messaging even there she found surprisingly rare usage of short forms such as "u" for "you", and as students got older, they began to write in more grammatical sentences. That is because they want to appear more adult, and they know how adults are expected to write. Clearly, teaching teens formal writing is still crucial, but texting probably isn't destroying their ability to learn it.

It is probably true that fewer kids are heavy readers compared with two generations ago, when cheap paperbacks boosted rates of reading. But even back then, a minority of people—perhaps 20%—were lifelong heavy readers, and it was cable TV not the internet, that struck a blow at that culture in the 1980s. Still, 15% or more of kids are found to be deeply bookish. In fact, the online world offers kids remarkable opportunities to become literate and creative because young people can now publish ideas not just to their friends, but to the world. And it turns out that when they write for strangers, their sense of "authentic audience" makes them work harder, push themselves further, and create powerful new communicative forms.

Few would deny that too much time online can be harmful. Some of the dangers are emotional: hurting someone from a distance is not the same as hurting them face to face. If we're lucky, the legal environment will change to make teenagers' online lives less likely to haunt them later on. Just last week, California passed a law allowing minors to demand that internet firms erase their digital past and the EU has considered similar legislation.

Distraction is also a serious issue. When kids switch from chat to music to homework, they are indeed likely to have trouble doing each task well. And studies show that pupils don't fact-check information online —"smart searching" is a skill schools need to teach urgently. It's also true that too much social networking and game playing can cut into schoolwork and sleep. This is precisely why parents still need to set firm boundaries around it, as with any other distraction.

So what's the best way to cope? The same boring old advice that applies to everything in parenting: moderation. Rebecca Eynon argues that it's key to model good behaviour. Parents who stare non-stop at their phones and don't read books are likely to breed kids who will do the same. As ever, we ought to be careful about our own behaviour.

careful.passage: In the history of horse racing, few horses have captured the affection of the British public like Red Rum. Today, three decades after his retirement, he is still one of the best-known and most beloved racehorses of all time. Red Rum was passed around to several owners before being purchased for Noel Le Mar. The agent who made the purchase was the now-legendary horse trainer Donald "Ginger" McCain. It wasn't apparent at the time, but Red Rum had a serious bone disease in his foot. For many horses (and many trainers) this would mean the end of a racing career before it even began. For Ginger and Red Rum, though, it was just an obstacle to greatness that had to be overcome. Red Rum's true talent came out in steeplechases(障碍赛马). His power, speed and jumping ability carried him to his first Grand National title in 1973. The very next year, Red Rum returned to take his second title. He was the first horse to take successive firsts since Reynoldstown in 1935-1936. Red Rum's spirit and grace had already begun to charm the leagues of Grand National fans. In the following two years, Red Rum lost out on the title, coming in second both times. When he returned in 1977 to try again, he was largely regarded as past his prime. He was 12 years old and not expected to place highly. He surprised sporting fans around the world when he came in a remarkable 25 lengths ahead of the nearest horse, taking his third Grand National win. To this day, Red Rum's third win is known as one of the greatest moments in horse racing history. Red Rum was headed for the Grand National once again in 1978 but suffered an injury in one of his heels shortly before the race. He was retired soon after, but his public life and fame by no means decreased with the end of his career. Red Rum traveled all over the country for various engagements. He often led pre-race parades at Aintree Racecourse and was a popular guest at charity benefits and public events.

careful.passage: People in business often make decisions based on their own personal feelings or instincts. It is quite horrifying to see people being guided by some unknown force. But how wise is it, really, to let your instincts drive your decisions? In the decision-making process, relying on instincts only makes sense when you have a vast experience to support you. Simply "feeling" that something is right or should be done is highly subjective and can drown you. On the other hand, there is a more rational approach to making decisions. Data and analysis have long been associated with informed decisions. These reduce the likelihood of errors and increase the chances of success. Big, systematic data is mostly the foundation of most of our decisions, personal and business alike. But with its extreme usability comes a complication: what do you do if you strongly feel something should not be done, even if the data insists that it should? This seemingly easy question is what drives the need to understand the relationship between instincts and data in the decision-making process. Without making things complicated, the solution to this dilemma is using data and instincts in conjunction to arrive at the best possible decisions. Instinctive decisions are always backed by previous experiences or information, which acknowledges that instinctive decisions have worked in the past. Decisions are not about making the choice and braving the consequences because you want to blindly trust your instincts. They are about combining your inner wisdom with the knowledge of systematic data to make the best decisions. Sometimes, rational analysis and data are impractical to be employed in certain situations. Absence of definitive criteria, and time and resource constraints, and novel situations are instances which limit the practicality of data. The only feasible option is to rely on what your instincts tell you. In these situations, instincts can help you make effective and quick decisions. Combining instinctive and rational analysis produces well-rounded decisions. It reduces the chances of making mistakes, and has increasingly become a favorite approach to decision-making among leaders of today.

translation.source: 改革开放以来，中国人民生活水平不断提高，这在人们的饮食 (diet)变化上得到充分体现 。如今，人们不 再满足于吃得饱，而是追求吃得更加安全、更加营养、更加健康，食物也愈来愈丰富多样，不再限于本地的农 产品。物流业 (logistics industry)的发展使人们很容易品尝到全国各地的特产。毫无疑问，食品质量与饮食结 构的改善为增进人们健康提供了有力的保障。
translation.reference: Since the reform and opening-up, the living standards of the Chinese people have improved steadily, which is fully reflected in the changes in people's diet. Today, people are no longer content with simply having enough to eat; instead, they pursue food that is safer, more nutritious and healthier. Food is also becoming more and more diverse, no longer being limited to local agricultural products. The development of the logistics industry makes it easy for people to taste specialties from all over the country. Undoubtedly, the improvement in food quality and diet structure provides a strong guarantee for improving people's health.
